preamble.summary: Ben Sira's personal conclusion in two parts: a thanksgiving prayer for deliverance from mortal danger (vv. 1-12), and an alphabetic acrostic poem about seeking wisdom from youth (vv. 13-30). The book ends with an invitation to acquire wisdom freely.
preamble.remarkable: The acrostic poem (vv. 13-30) was found in Hebrew at both Qumran (11QPsa) and Masada, confirming the book's original Hebrew composition. Verse 25 ('Acquire wisdom without money') anticipates Isaiah 55:1 and Jesus's 'freely you have received, freely give' (Matthew 10:8). This is Ben Sira's personal testimony — the only autobiographical passage from a named biblical author outside Paul.
preamble.friction: The Vulgate's chapter 51 contains some material not found in the Greek or Hebrew — Jerome may have drawn on a longer Aramaic/Hebrew tradition. The acrostic structure is invisible in Latin translation.
preamble.connections: Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22 (thanksgiving for deliverance), Isaiah 55:1 (come without money), Matthew 11:28-30 (take my yoke — Sirach's yoke of wisdom), 11QPsa (Qumran Psalms Scroll contains this acrostic).

verses.text_latin: Confitebor tibi Domine rex et conlaudabo te Deum salvatorem meum
verses.rendering: I will give thanks to you, Lord and King, and I will praise you, God my Savior.
translator_notes: Opening formula matches psalmic thanksgiving — confitebor (I will confess/give thanks) signals a todah psalm.

key_terms.note: Echoes Habakkuk 3:18 and anticipates Luke 1:47 (Mary's Magnificat: 'God my Savior')

verses.text_latin: Confitebor nomini tuo quoniam adiutor et protector factus es mihi
verses.rendering: I will give thanks to your name, for you have been my helper and protector,

verses.text_latin: et liberasti corpus meum a perditione a laqueo linguae iniquae et a labiis operantium mendacium et in conspectu adstantium factus es mihi adiutor
verses.rendering: and you have delivered my body from destruction, from the snare of a slanderous tongue, from lips that fashion lies — and in the presence of those who stood by, you became my helper.
translator_notes: Laqueo linguae iniquae (snare of a wicked tongue) — Ben Sira's crisis involved false accusation, not physical attack.

verses.text_latin: Et liberasti me secundum multitudinem misericordiae nominis tui a rugientibus praeparatis ad escam
verses.rendering: You delivered me, according to the abundance of your name's mercy, from those who roared, prepared to devour —

verses.text_latin: De manu quaerentium animam meam et de portis tribulationum quae circumdederunt me
verses.rendering: from the hand of those who sought my life, and from the gates of afflictions that surrounded me,

verses.text_latin: A pressura flammae quae circumdedit me et in medio ignis non sum aestuatus
verses.rendering: from the choking flame that encircled me — and in the midst of fire I was not burned,
translator_notes: Echoes Daniel 3 (the three in the furnace) — whether literal or metaphorical, the pattern of divine rescue is the same.

verses.text_latin: De altitudine ventris inferi et a lingua coinquinata et a verbo mendacii a rege iniquo et a lingua iniusta
verses.rendering: from the depth of the belly of Sheol, and from an unclean tongue, from lying speech, from an unjust king and a slanderous tongue.
translator_notes: Ventris inferi (belly of Sheol) — echoes Jonah 2:3. Death itself could not hold him.

key_terms.note: Jonah's 'belly of the fish/Sheol' echoed — near-death experience as descent to the underworld

verses.text_latin: Laudabit usque ad mortem anima mea Dominum
verses.rendering: My soul will praise the Lord even to death,

verses.text_latin: Et vita mea adpropinquans erat in inferno deorsum
verses.rendering: for my life was drawing near to Sheol below.

verses.text_latin: Circumdederunt me undique et non erat qui adiuvaret respiciens eram ad adiutorium hominum et non erat
verses.rendering: They surrounded me on every side, and there was no one to help; I looked for human aid, and there was none.

verses.text_latin: Memoratus sum misericordiae tuae Domine et operationis tuae quae a saeculo sunt
verses.rendering: Then I remembered your mercy, Lord, and your deeds from of old —

verses.text_latin: Quoniam eruis sustinentes te Domine et liberas eos de manibus gentium
verses.rendering: that you rescue those who wait for you, Lord, and deliver them from the hands of the nations.
translator_notes: Transition verse — from personal crisis to the universal principle: God delivers the patient.

verses.text_latin: Exaltasti super terram habitationem meam et pro morte defluente deprecatus sum
verses.rendering: You exalted my dwelling on the earth, and I prayed for deliverance from death.
translator_notes: Here begins the second section — the autobiographical wisdom poem (vv. 13-30 in the Hebrew acrostic).

verses.text_latin: Invocavi Dominum patrem Domini mei ut non derelinquat me in die tribulationis meae et in tempore superborum sine adiutorio
verses.rendering: I called upon the Lord, the Father of my Lord, not to forsake me in the day of trouble, in the time of the arrogant, when there is no help.
translator_notes: Patrem Domini mei — unusual formula. In Christian reading, 'Father of my Lord' anticipates Trinitarian language, though Ben Sira likely means 'Lord who is my master/father.'

verses.text_latin: Laudabo nomen tuum adsidue et conlaudabo illud in confessione et exaudita est oratio mea
verses.rendering: I will praise your name continually and sing it with thanksgiving, and my prayer was heard.

verses.text_latin: Et liberasti me de perditione et eripuisti me de tempore iniquo
verses.rendering: You delivered me from destruction and rescued me from the evil time.

verses.text_latin: Propterea confitebor et laudem dicam tibi et benedicam nomini Domini
verses.rendering: Therefore I will give thanks and praise to you, and bless the name of the Lord.
translator_notes: End of the thanksgiving; transition to the wisdom autobiography.

verses.text_latin: Cum adhuc iunior essem priusquam oberrarem quaesivi sapientiam palam in oratione mea
verses.rendering: While I was still young, before I went astray, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer.
translator_notes: Beginning of the acrostic autobiography. 'Before I went astray' — unusual honesty; Ben Sira admits youthful error.

verses.text_latin: Ante templum postulabam pro illa et usque in novissimis inquiram eam et effloruit tamquam praecox uva
verses.rendering: Before the temple I asked for her, and I will search for her to the end. She flourished like a ripening grape.

verses.text_latin: Laetatum est cor meum in ea ambulavit pes meus iter rectum a iuventute mea investigabam eam
verses.rendering: My heart rejoiced in her, my foot walked the straight path; from my youth I tracked her down.

verses.text_latin: Inclinavi modice aurem meam et excepi illam
verses.rendering: I inclined my ear a little and received her,

verses.text_latin: Et multam inveni in me ipso sapientiam et multum profeci in ea
verses.rendering: and I found much wisdom within myself, and I made great progress through her.

verses.text_latin: Danti mihi sapientiam dabo gloriam
verses.rendering: To the one who gives me wisdom I will give glory.

verses.text_latin: Consiliatus sum enim ut facerem illam et zelatus sum bonum et non confundar
verses.rendering: For I resolved to practice her, and I was zealous for the good, and I shall never be put to shame.

verses.text_latin: Conluctata est anima mea in illa et in faciendo eam confirmatus sum
verses.rendering: My soul wrestled with wisdom, and in practicing her I was strengthened.

verses.text_latin: Manus meas extendi in altum et insipientiam eius luxi
verses.rendering: I stretched out my hands on high, and I lamented my ignorance of her.

verses.text_latin: Animam meam direxi ad illam et in agnitione inveni eam
verses.rendering: I directed my soul toward her, and in understanding I found her.

verses.text_latin: Possedi cor cum illa ab initio propter hoc non derelinquar
verses.rendering: I possessed my heart with her from the beginning; therefore I shall not be forsaken.

verses.text_latin: Venter meus conturbatus est quaerendo illam propterea bonam possidebo possessionem
verses.rendering: My inmost self was stirred in seeking her; therefore I have gained a good possession.

verses.text_latin: Dedit mihi Dominus linguam mercedem meam et in ipsa laudabo eum
verses.rendering: The Lord gave me a tongue as my reward, and with it I will praise him.
translator_notes: Ben Sira's 'reward' is the gift of teaching — his tongue is his ministry. The book ends as it began: wisdom is for sharing.

key_terms.note: The teacher's reward is the ability to teach — wisdom received must be wisdom given. Anticipates 'freely you received, freely give' (Matt 10:8)

verses.text_latin: Adpropiate ad me indocti et congregate vos in domum disciplinae
verses.rendering: Draw near to me, you untaught, and lodge in the house of instruction.
translator_notes: The final invitation — wisdom's door is open. Domum disciplinae (house of instruction) is the bet midrash, the school.

key_terms.note: Hebrew bet midrash — the synagogue school. Ben Sira's own academy where this book was taught.

verses.text_latin: Quid adhuc retardatis et quid dicitis in his animae vestrae sitim habentes vehementer
verses.rendering: Why do you still hold back? Why do you say anything about these things, when your souls thirst so greatly?

verses.text_latin: Aperui os meum et locutus sum conparate vobis sine argento sapientiam
verses.rendering: I opened my mouth and said: Acquire wisdom for yourselves without money.
translator_notes: Sine argento (without money) — wisdom cannot be bought, only sought. Echoes Isaiah 55:1 'come without money' and anticipates Matthew 10:8.

key_terms.note: The democratization of wisdom — available to all regardless of wealth. Counter-cultural in the ancient world where education required patronage.

verses.text_latin: Collum vestrum subicite iugo et suscipiat anima vestra disciplinam in proximo enim est invenire eam
verses.rendering: Submit your neck to the yoke, and let your soul receive instruction; she is near at hand to find.
translator_notes: Iugo (yoke) — Jesus's 'my yoke is easy' (Matthew 11:29-30) directly echoes this invitation. Ben Sira's yoke of wisdom becomes Christ's yoke of discipleship.

key_terms.note: The wisdom-yoke tradition: Sirach 6:24-25, 51:26, then Matthew 11:29. Torah as yoke → Wisdom as yoke → Christ as yoke.

verses.text_latin: Videte oculis vestris quia modicum laboravi et inveni mihi multam requiem
verses.rendering: See with your own eyes that I labored but a little and found for myself much rest.
translator_notes: Requiem (rest) — the sage's reward is rest/peace. Connects to Matthew 11:28 'I will give you rest' and Hebrews 4 'sabbath rest.'

verses.text_latin: Adsumite disciplinam in multo numero argenti et copiosum aurum possidete in ea
verses.rendering: Acquire instruction with a great sum of silver, and you will gain much gold through her.
translator_notes: Paradox with v. 33 — wisdom is 'without money' yet worth any price. Not contradiction but emphasis: wisdom cannot be bought, but it is worth everything.

verses.text_latin: Laetetur anima vestra in misericordia eius et non confundemini in laude ipsius
verses.rendering: Let your soul rejoice in his mercy, and you will not be put to shame in praising him.

verses.text_latin: Operamini opus vestrum ante tempus et dabit vobis mercedem vestram in tempore suo
verses.rendering: Do your work before the appointed time, and in his own time he will give you your reward.
translator_notes: The final word of Sirach: faithful work now, divine reward in God's timing. A fitting conclusion to 51 chapters of practical wisdom.
